%%
%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the
%% article.
\begin{abstract}
Online moral discussions often converge on a prevailing verdict, yet agreement can obscure how dissenting voices are received and what alternative moral reasons they offer. We investigate how minority judgments are evaluated, how others respond to them, and whether exposure to dissent broadens the range of moral reasons readers take into account in Reddit’s r/AmItheAsshole. Minority judgments receive lower scores but attract more replies and deeper discussions than majority judgments, with larger differences in high-agreement discussions. Blaming dissent against a defending majority attracts more replies and deeper discussion than defending dissent against a blaming majority. Replies to minority judgments predominantly challenge them, whereas replies to majority judgments predominantly offer support. We further examine whether direct replies introduce moral reasons absent from their parent comments. Finally, a randomized controlled study tests whether exposure to different views changes people’s moral judgments and perceptions of online discussions, comparing two majority threads with one majority and one minority thread. Together, these analyses connect the reception of dissent with the moral reasons exchanged around it and readers’ responses to encountering opposing views.
\end{abstract}
